Alternatively, if the buyer chooses to enter a feedback message, they input their feedback, which is then sent to the online group purchasing system for format verification. The system checks the format of the feedback message. If the format is invalid, an error message is shown to the buyer. If the format is valid, the feedback message is submitted successfully, and the system displays a confirmation message to the buyer. This marks the end of the feedback submission path.

Throughout the process, the buyer interacts with the system, and the system provides feedback and guidance based on the actions taken by the buyer.

The graduation process begins with the Registrar's Office running a list of potential graduates. Once this list is compiled, the Registrar's Office sends an email to these potential graduates to inform them of their status.

Following this, students have the opportunity to declare their intention to graduate. Once a student declares their intention, the Registrar's Office pulls audits from the eDDS system to verify the student's eligibility. After retrieving the audits, the Registrar's Office collects the student folders and places them in Holly's file for further processing.

Next, the Registrar's Office sends graduation verification documents to the respective schools. These documents are then reviewed and approved by the Department Head. If the Department Head approves the verifications, the process continues to a decision point.

At this decision point, the Registrar's Office checks if there are any problems with the verification. If there are no problems, the process proceeds with sending the documents to Jane Doe. If there are issues, the documents are sent to MEB for further review.

If the documents are sent to MEB, another decision point arises to determine if the substitutions resolve the problem. If the problem is resolved, the updated verification is filed, and the process continues. If the problem is not resolved, a letter is sent to the student, with copies to the advisor and program chair, and a note is made on the yellow list.

Finally, the process concludes with the Registrar's Office adding or dropping students as needed and sending out verifications as required. This marks the end of the graduation process.

The process begins when the Customer Admin at Singapore Management University receives an email order from a customer. The Customer Admin then creates an order in the Order Tracking System (OTS). After creating the order, the Customer Admin generates and prints a pick sheet using the Warehouse Information System (WIS). This pick sheet is then passed to the Warehouse Supervisor.

The Warehouse Supervisor assigns the pick sheet to the Warehouse Operators. The Warehouse Operators review the pick sheet and select the necessary equipment for picking. They proceed to the pick location and search the surrounding area for the goods.

At this point, there is a decision to be made: if the goods are found, which happens 75% of the time, the Warehouse Operator picks the required quantity. If the goods are not found, which occurs 25% of the time, the process ends with the goods not being found.

If the goods are picked, another decision is made: if the quantity is available, which is the case 80% of the time, the Warehouse Operator packs the goods onto a package. If the quantity is not available, which happens 20% of the time, the Warehouse Operator writes the shortage on the pick sheet and passes it to the Warehouse Supervisor. The Warehouse Supervisor updates the WIS of the shortage and informs the Customer Admin via phone. The Customer Admin then updates the shortage backlog in the OTS delivery manifest, and the order delivery is backlogged.

If the goods are packed, the Warehouse Operator moves the package to the loading area and passes the pick sheet to the Shipping Operator. The Shipping Operator reviews the pick sheet with the WIS and enters the order number into the OTS to view the delivery manifest. They then print the delivery label and manifest from the OTS, paste the delivery label onto the package, and dispatch the delivery manifest and package to the driver.

Finally, the Shipping Operator prints the invoice from the OTS and prepares an email to the customer for dispatch to the mail outbox, marking the end of the process with the package being dispatched.

The business process begins with the OPC Acceptance, which is initiated by PAL and the team. This marks the start of the process.

Following this, a Kick-Off Meeting is conducted by PAL and the team to set the stage for the project. After the meeting, the process splits into two parallel paths.

In the first path, PAL and the team carry out a FacMan and EHS evaluation. This task leads to the ECD and Contractor Bids task, also handled by PAL and the team.

Simultaneously, in the second path, the Integration team conducts a Site Survey. This task produces a Site Survey Form. After the survey, the Integration team prepares the Contractor SOW, which results in a Contractor SOW document. The process then moves to the Integrator SOW task, also managed by the Integration team, generating an Integrator SOW document.

Meanwhile, the Integration team performs an Integrator Deep Dive, resulting in an Integrator Checklist. This task leads to the Request Equip Quotes task, managed by PAL and the team. After requesting quotes, the team performs a Price Check, which then leads to the Order Equipment task.

The Design team then creates a Design Proposal, resulting in a Full Design (99%) document. This proposal is followed by the Proposal Acceptance or Decline task, managed by PAL and the team.

At this point, a decision is made. If the proposal is declined, the process ends with the task "Close Project - Charge for Design Labor," handled by PAL and the team. If the proposal is accepted, the process loops back to the Kick-Off Meeting, indicating a continuation or iteration of the process.

The process begins with the task of scheduling a delivery, which is handled by the Assembler/Packer in the warehouse. Once the delivery is scheduled, the next step is to check the delivery date.

The Assembler/Packer checks if the order is due for delivery. If the order is not due, it is kept in the delayed file. After being placed in the delayed file, the process moves to updating the priority shipping status. If the order is due for delivery, the process directly proceeds to updating the priority shipping status.

After updating the priority shipping status, the Assembler/Packer packs the order. Following the packing, the delivery method is checked to determine if the customer will pick up the order.

If the customer is picking up the order, the Assembler/Packer arranges for customer self pick-up, and the process concludes with the order being completed. If the customer is not picking up the order, the delivery location is checked to see if it is a local delivery.

For local deliveries, the Assembler/Packer contacts the driver, and the customer signs the docket. The process then ends with the order being delivered and completed. If the delivery is not local, the Assembler/Packer contacts delivery services, and the process concludes with the order being delivered and completed.

The flight booking process begins with the customer initiating the process. The customer starts by placing a booking request. This request is then received by the travel agent, who proceeds to book the flight request. The travel agent views the details of the booking and analyzes the specifics of the flight. Following this, the travel agent checks whether the flight is available.

At this point, the process reaches a decision point. If the flight seat is unavailable, the travel agent finds that the seat is unavailable and provides the customer with other booking options. The customer then receives the new offer for booking and analyzes it. If the customer is satisfied, they notify the agent about the seat settlement.

If the flight seat is available, the travel agent books the seat in the flight. The customer then proceeds to make the payment. Once the payment is made, the travel agent confirms that the payment has been acquired.

Finally, the process concludes with the customer, marking the end of the flight booking process.

The process begins with the university initiating the cooperation process. The university writes a cooperation request and then sends this request to the business partner. The cooperation request document is associated with this task.

Upon receiving the cooperation request, the business partner evaluates it. At this point, the business partner must decide whether the request is acceptable or not. If the request is deemed not acceptable, the business partner denies the request and subsequently sends a denial letter to the university. This results in the cooperation not being established.

If the business partner finds the request acceptable, they proceed to accept it. Following acceptance, the business partner has another decision to make: whether to accept the request with comments or without comments. If the request is accepted with comments, the business partner sends these comments back to the university. The university then receives these comments and processes them.

If the request is accepted without comments, the process moves directly to the next step. In both cases, whether comments are sent or not, the university proceeds to establish the cooperation. The contracts document is associated with the task of establishing cooperation.

Finally, the process concludes with either the cooperation being successfully established or not, depending on the decisions made throughout the process. The process ends with the university acknowledging the outcome.

The process begins with an applicant sending a message to the Tennis Volley Club. This message is received by Jane Doe, who is responsible for handling the application process.

Jane Doe starts by making a membership decision. If the decision is positive, she stamps the application with "new member" and the date. She then transmits a letter to herself, Jane Doe, confirming the new membership status. Following this, she adds the new member to the club's records.

Next, Jane Doe calculates the membership fee. After calculating the fee, she writes down the amount and prepares an invoice at home. She then sends out the invoices to the new member.

Simultaneously, Jane Doe prints the membership card and sends it to the new member. This marks the end of the process for a successful membership application.

If the membership decision is negative, Jane Doe sends a negative response back to the applicant, concluding the process for that application.

Throughout the process, Jane Doe ensures that all documents are recorded and archived appropriately. The process concludes once the membership card is sent, or a negative response is communicated to the applicant.

The process begins with a student initiating the task of booking items using the intranet. After booking, the student checks the availability time for the items. If the items are available, the student proceeds to book them. Next, the student checks the availability of a delivery slot with the staff. If a slot is available, the student books the staff delivery time and the estate department receives the booked items and delivery time details.

The estate department then delivers the booked items based on the delivery slot. Once the student receives the booked items, they return them after the event. The estate department checks the condition of the returned items. If the items are returned in good condition, the estate department updates the items' availability chart, marking the end of the process.

If the items are not available initially, or if no delivery slot is available, the process ends for the student without further actions. If the items are returned in poor condition, the estate department notifies the student of a penalty. The student then pays the penalty, and the process ends for the student.

The process begins with the company initiating the registration of a complaint. The company then assesses how many parts are affected by the issue. Following this, the supplier gathers necessary information from the company to proceed with investigating the complaint.

Once the investigation is complete, the supplier reaches a decision point. If the decision is to design a changed part, the supplier proceeds to do so and then conducts a plausibility test on the changed part. Alternatively, if the decision is to design a new part, the supplier designs the new part and performs a plausibility test on it.

After the plausibility tests, the supplier either changes the part number (version) for the changed part or creates a new part number for the new part. The company then saves the new drawings and numbers in the system.

Next, the supplier provides a release date and informs the production team. At this point, another decision is made. If the new parts need to be manufactured, the supplier proceeds with manufacturing them. Otherwise, the company gets the release date from the supplier and informs the production team, leading to the release of the part, which concludes the process.

The process begins with the task of preparing the dough. Once the dough is prepared, the next step is to cover it with a thin film. After covering the dough, it is allowed to settle. This settling period is followed by a waiting time of 2-3 hours.

After the waiting period, two tasks occur simultaneously. The first task is to place the dough on a tray for baking. The second task involves starting the oven. Once the oven is started, it is pre-heated to 450 degrees Fahrenheit.

After pre-heating, the dough is placed in the oven for baking. The oven temperature is then reduced to 400 degrees Fahrenheit, and the dough is baked for 10 minutes. Following this, the temperature is further reduced to 350 degrees Fahrenheit, and the baking continues for an additional 5 minutes.

After the baking time, the oven checks if the croissants are completely baked. If the croissants are ready, they are removed from the oven. If not, the process of reducing the temperature to 350 degrees Fahrenheit and baking for 5 minutes is repeated.

Once the croissants are removed from the oven, they are served as delicious croissants, marking the end of the process.

The business process begins with the Sales department receiving an external forecast through a message. The Sales department then analyzes this external forecast data. After the initial analysis, they proceed to evaluate the feasibility of the forecast. Once the feasibility analysis is complete, the Sales department prepares for a forecast approval meeting. This preparation leads to the completion of the external forecast analysis.

Simultaneously, the process involves the Affiliate, who receives a forecast proposal from the Supply chain department. The Affiliate starts by analyzing the forecast proposal. Following this, they collect and analyze local market data, which is stored in a local market data repository. The Affiliate then assesses the acceptability of the forecast proposal.

At this point, a decision is made based on the assessment. If the forecast proposal is accepted, the Affiliate makes a new forecast based on the local data. If the proposal is not accepted, the Affiliate proceeds to accept the forecast proposal as it is. Regardless of the decision, the Affiliate sends the external forecast to the Sales department and attends the forecast approval meeting. This concludes the process for the Affiliate with the delivery of the external forecast being completed.

The process begins when the Talent Seek Coordinator closes an application. The coordinator then checks the application to determine if it is in digital format. If the application is digital, the coordinator prints it. If it is not digital, the process moves directly to checking the application for completeness.

After printing the digital application, the coordinator also checks it for completeness. At this point, the coordinator assesses whether any information is missing from the application. If information is missing, the coordinator sends the application to be discarded by the Administration & Clerical Staff. This concludes with the application being retained by the staff.

If no information is missing, the coordinator sends the application forward. The application is then packaged appropriately by the coordinator. Once packaged, the application is sent to the Recruitment Manager, who receives it. The process concludes with the Recruitment Manager processing the application.

The process begins with the secretary at the dermatologist's office starting the workflow by making an appointment for a consultation. Once the appointment is set, the dermatologist gathers necessary information from the patient. Following this, the dermatologist takes a sample from the patient and sends it to the lab for analysis.

Simultaneously, the lab receives the sample and begins analyzing it. Once the analysis is complete, the lab sends the results back to the dermatologist.

Back at the dermatologist's office, upon receiving the lab results, the dermatologist makes a diagnosis. After the diagnosis, two tasks occur at the same time: the dermatologist contacts the patient to discuss the results and updates the patient's information.

Next, the dermatologist checks the patient's anesthetization status and performs a preoperative screening. If everything is in order, the dermatologist proceeds with the surgery.

After the surgery, the secretary schedules post-treatment checks. During these checks, the dermatologist performs two tasks simultaneously: checking the patient's wounds and removing stitches. Finally, the dermatologist conducts a final check on the patient, concluding the process.

The procurement process begins with the ERP system automatically correlating purchase orders, invoices, and receptions. This task is performed by the ERP system of the company.

Next, the process checks for any problems. If no problems are found, the ERP system automatically creates a list of payments due. Following this, an alert for capital is sent by the ERP system.

After sending the alert, the Accounts Payable (AP) department checks the payment status. If the payment is approved, the AP department proceeds to make the payment, concluding this branch of the process.

If a problem is detected during the initial check, an automatic email is sent to the PA with details of the issue. The AP department then calls the responsible party to fix the issue. After this, another check is performed. If the issue is resolved, the process returns to the ERP system to create the list of payments due. If the issue is not resolved, a rejection is sent on the ERP system, ending this branch of the process.

In cases where the payment status check by the AP department results in a rejection, the AP department fixes the appealing issue and then makes the payment, concluding this branch of the process.

The process begins with a customer starting their interaction with the food catering service system. The customer first browses the webpage or application. After browsing, the system verifies if the customer is a member. If the customer is a member, they proceed to enable their location. If not, the customer registers as a member and sends an email confirmation. The system then verifies the email. If the email is invalid, an error message is sent, and the process ends. If the email is valid, the customer enables their location.

Once the location is enabled, the system displays nearby caterers to the customer. The customer selects a caterer and places an order. The caterer then prepares the ordered food and delivers it to the customer. Upon receiving the food, the customer makes a payment and confirms that the order has been received. Finally, the system updates the order status, and the process concludes.

The process begins with the Communications department at Bosch receiving new business figures. Once these figures are received, the Communications department sends them to the relevant departments, such as HR.

Upon receiving the new business figures, the HR department at Bosch checks if there is a new intern involved in the process. If there is a new intern, the HR department shows the intern how the process works. This involves showing them the location of the log-in information and explaining the process. After this, HR answers any questions the intern might have.

If there is no new intern, the HR department proceeds to handle the task themselves. They start by opening the Excel file containing the business figures. Next, they check the online resources that need updating with the new figures. After identifying the necessary updates, HR logs in and updates the business figures online. Once the updates are made, they mark the updated resources as done in the file.

After either path, whether involving an intern or not, the HR department performs a random check to ensure the business numbers are correct. Finally, the process concludes with the HR department finishing the update of business figures online.

The process begins with a clerk starting the procedure. The first task for the clerk is to receive a petition inquiry. Once the inquiry is received, the clerk checks the required particulars of the petition to ensure all necessary information is present.

After verifying the particulars, the clerk reviews the nature of the petition to understand its context and details. At this point, a decision is made based on the petition's expressed value. If the expressed value is less than 50.0, the clerk proceeds to find the expressed value and then catches if the petition is considered high touch. Following this, the clerk notifies the customer about the petition status.

If the expressed value is greater than 50.0, the clerk handles the petition by expressing the customer's petition and then mentions any requirements needed. After this, the clerk also notifies the customer that the petition is being handled.

Finally, the process concludes with the clerk ensuring that the customer is informed about the handling of their petition, marking the end of the process.

The process begins when there is a need for a research paper. The first step is to go to the library. Once at the library, the next task is to open the index of research papers on a computer. After accessing the index, the task is to find the desired research paper on the computer.

Following this, the availability of the research paper is checked. At this point, there is a decision to be made based on the availability of the paper. If the research paper is available, the next step is to note the shelf number. After noting the shelf number, the research paper is picked from the shelf. The student then presents their student ID to receive the research paper.

If the research paper is not available, the student logs in with their student user ID on the computer. They then proceed to order the research paper. After ordering, the student notes the order details and logs out from the system.

Regardless of whether the research paper was picked from the shelf or ordered, the final step is to leave the library. This marks the end of the process.

The process begins with a student initiating the sequence. The student starts by checking the timetable. If there is no problem with the timetable, the student continues to use it. This marks the end of the process for the student.

If the student identifies a problem with the timetable, they report it to the Programme Leader for correction. The Programme Leader receives the report and proceeds to identify and confirm the error reported by the student. Once the error is confirmed, the Programme Leader configures the system by inputting the necessary corrections into the Personnel System.

The Personnel System, managed by the Programme Leader, is then involved in the process. It connects to the Timetable System, which performs a self-error check. If the Timetable System detects an error, it redoes the timetable and corrects any mistakes. After corrections, the system plans and estimates the timetable, generating a new timetable from forecasted data.

The newly generated timetable is then checked again by the Timetable System for any errors. If no errors are found, the process returns to the Programme Leader, who submits the corrected timetable back to the student for rechecking. The student then reassesses the timetable to ensure all issues have been resolved.

If the student finds that the problem persists, they resend the timetable back to the Programme Leader, and the process continues until the timetable is correct. If the student confirms that the timetable is now correct, they continue to use it, concluding the process.

The business process begins when a client brings in their tax return information to the Tax Return Department. The Front Desk Administrator logs the receipt of this information into the Practice Management system. After logging, the information is deposited into the assigned preparer's inbox.

The Preparer then picks up the documents from the inbox and logs the return as "In process" in the Practice Management system. Following this, the Preparer orders and sorts the documentation. Once organized, the Preparer inputs the information into the Lacerte tax preparer software.

Next, the Preparer logs the return as "ready for review" in the Practice Management system. The return is then logged as "in review" by the Reviewer, who proceeds to review the return.

During the review, the Reviewer checks if the documents are complete. If the information is complete, the process continues with the Preparer ordering and sorting the documentation again. If the information is not complete, the Preparer contacts the client to request additional information and logs the return as "on hold." This marks the end of the process for incomplete returns.

For returns that are complete, the Reviewer assesses the return. If there is an issue that requires a small fix, the Reviewer adjusts the return and signs off on it. If the issue requires rework, the Reviewer notifies the Preparer of the adjustments needed, and the process loops back to logging the return as "In process."

If the return is deemed okay, the Reviewer signs off on it. After signing off, the Reviewer logs the return as "reviewed" in the Practice Management system.

The process concludes with the Front Desk Administrator filing the return and logging it as "filed" in the Practice Management system. Finally, the customer is notified that a copy of the return can be picked up, marking the end of the process.

The process begins with a credit card application initiated by the account executive. The account executive fills out the application form and makes a copy of the applicant's ID. Once these tasks are completed, the process moves to the analyst.

The analyst performs a credit bureau check. Based on the results of this check, there are two possible paths. If the credit is deemed good, the analyst calculates the applicant's debt level. If the credit is deemed bad, the analyst denies the application, and the process moves to the account executive, who informs the client of the denial. This concludes the process for denied applications.

If the debt level calculation shows the applicant is suitable, the analyst opens an account in the system. The analyst then calculates the applicant's credit capacity and assigns a credit limit. After assigning the credit limit, the process returns to the operator, who prints the credit card.

The printed card is then handed over to the account executive, who delivers it to the client, marking the end of the process for approved applications.

The process begins when a customer decides they want to order an airplane. The customer starts by providing their personal data. Once this information is provided, two tasks occur simultaneously: the customer's personal data is stored, and the customer begins choosing specific features for the airplane. 

The customer selects a bar, the number of seats, and the amount of water to be included. They also choose the color of the airplane. After these selections, the customer checks the specifications to ensure everything is correct. If the customer wants to add more features, they enter additional information and recheck the specifications. If no further additions are needed, the customer sends the finalized specifications.

Once the specifications are sent, the airplane manufacturer receives them. The manufacturer then sends the requirements to the appropriate teams. The manufacturing teams receive the request and proceed to build and send the necessary pieces to the airplane manufacturer.

Upon receiving the pieces, the airplane manufacturer assembles the interior of the airplane. After assembly, the airplane undergoes a flight test. Following the test, a test report is automatically created. This report is then sent to both the airplane manufacturer and the customer simultaneously.

The customer receives the test report and, after reviewing it, the airplane is delivered to them. Upon receiving the airplane, the customer sends a confirmation back to the manufacturer. Once the confirmation is received, the manufacturer prepares the bill, marking the end of the process.

The process begins with a student at Punjab University initiating the procedure. The first step involves the student checking their financial scholarship letter. Once this is done, the student proceeds to send their application.

After the application is sent, the college administration receives the scholarship application. The administration then examines the academic papers submitted by the student. Following this examination, the administration compiles a list of selected applicants.

The process then moves to the committee, which starts interviewing the applicants. At this point, a decision is made. If the committee detects that an applicant is not qualified, they proceed to decline the applicant's application. This decision leads to the college administration publishing the names on the list.

If the committee determines that an applicant is qualified, the process continues with the college administration sanctioning the scholarship. After sanctioning, the administration publishes the name on the list.

The process concludes with the college administration finalizing the publication of the names on the list, marking the end of the procedure.

The process begins with Planner 2 identifying the need for Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). The first task involves exporting existing stock data, which is then used to update the stocks in a document labeled "KPI Yesterday." This document is associated with the task of updating stocks.

Next, Planner 2 copies sheets 1 and 2, which are then pasted into the "KPI Yesterday" document. Following this, the document's name is changed to "KPI Today."

Planner 2 then updates information about the backlog, which involves a document labeled "Backlog in Transit." After this, Planner 2 checks the column labeled "New products." This leads to a decision point where Planner 2 determines if there are new products.

If there are new products, Planner 2 exports and updates the relevant information. If there are no new products, the process moves directly to updating the "OTIF" column. The "OTIF Central Planning" document is associated with this task.

Subsequently, Planner 2 updates production orders, which involves a data store labeled "SAP." After updating production orders, Planner 2 updates the availability of components.

The next task is to mark priorities, which leads to disclosing the file for other planners. This file is stored in a data store labeled "Sharepoint."

Finally, the process concludes with the KPIs being published, marking the end of the process.

The business process begins with the Sales Department receiving an order. Once the order is received, the Sales Department processes it. After processing, a decision is made by the Sales Department to either accept or reject the order. If the order is rejected, the Sales Department marks the order as rejected, and the process ends there.

If the order is accepted, the Sales Department sends a message to both the Storehouse and the Engineering Department to initiate their respective tasks. The Storehouse begins by processing the part list. Following this, the Storehouse checks the quantity of the required parts. At this point, a decision is made based on the availability of the parts. If the parts are available, the Storehouse reserves them and confirms that all parts are successfully reserved. This confirmation is then sent to the Engineering Department.

If the parts are not available, the Storehouse places a back order for the parts and waits for them to arrive. Once the parts arrive, the Storehouse rechecks the quantity of the required parts, and the process repeats until all parts are available and reserved.

Simultaneously, the Engineering Department prepares for the assembly of the bicycle. Once the confirmation of all parts being reserved is received from the Storehouse, the Engineering Department proceeds with the assembly of the bicycle.

After the bicycle is assembled, the Sales Department takes over to handle the shipping of the bicycle. Finally, the process concludes with the successful shipping of the bicycle, marking the end of the process.

The process begins when an operator encounters an error. The operator's first task is to notify the occurrence of the error. This notification is then received by a supervisor.

The supervisor then asks the operator if a screenshot is necessary. If the operator decides that a screenshot is needed, they include it in the documentation. The screenshot is then associated with the error data. Regardless of whether a screenshot is included, the operator proceeds to send the problem information, which includes the error data, to the supervisor.

Once the supervisor receives the problem information, they open a ticket. The supervisor then determines if the software involved is EVO. If it is EVO, the supervisor fills out a form and sends a report to the SAP system, generating a SAP report. If the software is not EVO, the supervisor enters the help desk portal, selects the software, describes the problem, and sends an internal report, which results in the creation of a helpdesk ticket.

The internal support team receives the error report, marking the end of the process for them. Meanwhile, the process also concludes for the supervisor after sending the report or internal report, depending on the software involved.

The process begins with a customer being welcomed in the showroom of the Music Store. The showroom staff then shows the products to the customer, providing professional insights into each product to assist the customer in making an informed decision.

Following this, the customer reaches a decision point regarding their purchase. If the customer decides not to purchase, the visit ends. However, if the customer decides to proceed with the purchase, the showroom staff leads the customer to the cashier for payment.

Once the payment is completed, a transaction number is issued to the customer. This transaction number is then forwarded to the warehouse manager by the warehouse team.

The warehouse team examines the transaction receipt. If the receipt is rejected, the transaction receipt is returned. If the receipt is accepted, the warehouse team prepares the package for the customer.

After the package is prepared, the process reaches another decision point at the sales center. The customer can choose between self-pickup or home delivery. If the customer opts for self-pickup, the package is prepared for the customer to collect. If the customer chooses home delivery, the package is dispatched to the customer's address.

Finally, the process concludes with the end of the transaction, marking the completion of the customer's purchase journey at the Music Store.

The process begins with an employee initiating the task of purchasing work supplies. After the purchase, the employee checks the account status. At this point, a decision is made regarding whether an existing account is available. If there is an existing account, the process moves to an automatic approval review. If there is no existing account, the employee creates a new account and then proceeds to the automatic approval review.

Following the automatic approval review, the process checks if the purchase amount is under $200. If it is under $200, the reimbursement is approved, and the process waits for up to 7 days before the employee checks for an approval in-process email. If the purchase amount is equal to or over $200, the request is sent to a supervisor for approval.

If the supervisor approves the request, they send an approval notification, and the process continues with the reimbursement approval. If the supervisor rejects the request, they send a rejection notification via email, and the process ends.

After the employee checks for the approval in-process email, the process waits for 30 days before the employee checks the status. Once the status is checked, the request is marked as finished, and the process ends. If the request is rejected at any point, the employee receives a rejection notification email, and the process concludes.

The process begins when a reader decides they want to read a new book. The reader first considers if they have a specific book in mind. If they do not have a book in mind, they will ask friends for recommendations and then return to the initial consideration of whether they have a book in mind.

If the reader has a book in mind, they will check the availability of the book in the New Jane Doe Library's catalog through the NYPL website. If the book is available, the reader will proceed to reserve the book. The NYPL website will then confirm the reservation, and the reader will be asked if they have a library card.

If the reader does not have a library card, they will submit a library card application through the NYPL website. The application will be processed, and a branch librarian will issue a library card to the reader. Once the reader has a library card, they can pick up the reserved book.

If the book is not available in the catalog, a branch librarian will provide assistance. The librarian will identify an alternate book suggestion and reserve it for the reader. The reservation will then be confirmed by the NYPL website, and the reader will be asked if they have a library card, following the same steps as before.

Finally, once the reader has picked up the book, they can proceed to read it, concluding the process.

The process begins with the Procurement team at Winter Company initiating a request for quotation. This task involves gathering price and quality information from potential suppliers.

Once the quotations are received, the Procurement team compares the overall quality and price of the offers. This comparison helps in deciding whether to proceed with a purchase.

The decision point follows, where the Procurement team evaluates if the offers meet their requirements. If the decision is "Yes," they proceed to create a purchase order. If the decision is "No," they return to the initial step of requesting quotations.

After creating the purchase order, the Procurement team sends it to the supplier. The supplier then receives the purchase order and decides whether to accept it. If the supplier accepts the order, they prepare the goods for shipment. If the supplier rejects the order, they send an order rejection message back to the Procurement team, ending the process with an order rejection.

If the supplier accepts the order, they proceed to create an invoice and send it to the Procurement team. Upon receiving the invoice, the Procurement team makes the payment to the supplier.

Once the payment is received, the supplier ships the goods and sends a delivery order to the Procurement team. Upon receiving the delivery order, the process concludes successfully with the order being fulfilled.

The process begins when a member initiates a request to borrow equipment. The member starts by asking for the equipment. Once the request is made, the property manager checks the availability of the requested equipment.

At this point, the process encounters a decision point where the property manager determines if the equipment is available. If the equipment is available, the property manager proceeds to fill in a borrow form. This form is then associated with the member, who must sign it. After the member signs the borrow form, the property manager borrows the equipment on behalf of the member.

If the equipment is not available, the process ends with the property manager indicating that the equipment is not available.

Once the equipment is borrowed, the process waits until the borrowing period ends. When the borrowing time is over, the member returns the equipment.

Upon return, the property manager controls the state of the equipment. Another decision point arises here: the property manager checks if the equipment is in good condition. If the equipment is in good condition, the property manager writes a return record, and the process concludes.

If the equipment is not in good condition, the property manager quantifies the damage. The member is then required to pay for the damage. After the payment is made, the property manager updates the inventory, and the process ends with the return record being written.

Throughout the process, the borrow form and inventory are managed as data objects, ensuring that all necessary documentation is maintained and updated accordingly.

The process begins when an employee identifies that a data breach has occurred. The employee's first action is to inform the relevant parties about the data breach. Following this, the Project Manager or Project Delivery Lead gathers detailed information about the data breach.

Once the information is collected, the Data Protection Officer (DPO) documents the data breach. After documentation, the DPO notifies the Data Controller about the incident. The next step involves the DPO evaluating the risk associated with the data breach.

At this point, a decision is made based on the risk evaluation. If the incident is determined to have a low risk, the DPO proceeds to handle the incident directly. This involves taking actions to prevent future occurrences, after which the incident is closed.

If the incident is not considered low risk, the DPO triggers a Business Continuity Management (BCM) meeting. The BCM team is then responsible for informing the group about the situation. The team engages in decision-making regarding the remediation of the data breach. Following this, the BCM team takes actions necessary for remediation.

After the remediation actions are completed, the process moves to implementing actions for future prevention. Finally, the incident is closed, marking the end of the process.

The process begins when an employee acquires a travel request form. The first task for the employee is to provide a justification for the travel. Once the justification is provided, the employee must then specify the relevant travel dates. Following this, the employee is required to estimate the travel costs.

At this point, the process reaches a decision point. The employee must choose between two options: either they research the costs themselves or they get assistance from a travel assistant (TA) to research the costs. If the employee decides to research the costs themselves, they proceed to provide an estimated accommodation cost, followed by an estimated air fare cost, and finally, an estimated cost for meals and incidentals. After these estimates are provided, the employee must then estimate any event fees associated with the travel.

If the employee opts to get assistance from a TA, they must first contact the TA for an informal meeting, which is done via email. The TA then provides the estimated travel costs, which the employee receives.

After receiving the estimated travel costs, the process reaches another decision point. The employee must determine whether there are any private travel dates within the trip. If there are no private travel dates, the employee confirms this. If there are private travel dates, the employee receives the estimated costs for the private travel.

Once the decision regarding private travel dates is made, the employee addresses the request for the travel form to their supervisor. The form is then dropped into an internal mailbox. The process concludes when the completed request for travel form is sent via internal mail to the employee's supervisor at No Particular University (NPU).

The process begins when the Installation Supervisor at Custom-Build Electric Campervans (CEC) receives a request for quotation (RFQ). Upon receiving this request, the Installation Supervisor organizes the necessary teams to proceed with the project.

Once the teams are organized, the process splits into two parallel tasks. The first task involves Team A, led by the Installation Supervisor, focusing on the foundation and footing work. Simultaneously, Team B, also under the supervision of the Installation Supervisor, handles the plumbing and electrical connections.

After Team A completes the foundation and footing, the Delivery Team prepares the shed for delivery. This task concludes with the shed being delivered to the designated location.

Meanwhile, Team B's task of plumbing and electrical connections leads to an inspection by the Local Authority. The Local Authority inspects the materials and electrical units to ensure compliance with standards.

If the inspection is approved, the process concludes with the installation of the electric charging system. However, if the inspection is not approved, Team C, under the Installation Supervisor, is tasked with rectifying the identified issues. After rectification, the Local Authority re-inspects the work.

Following the re-inspection, a decision is made. If the work is approved, the process ends with the successful installation of the electric charging system. If not approved, the process loops back to Team C for further rectification and subsequent re-inspection.

Throughout this process, the Customer initiates the sequence by sending a request to the Installation Supervisor, marking the start of the entire workflow.

At the end of each month, the process begins with a part-time employee scanning their thumb on a fingerprint system. This action is followed by the manager reviewing the employee's timecard to check the time and date of their work.

Next, the manager calculates the hourly pay for the employee. After this calculation, the manager checks if the hours worked exceed 160. If the hours are greater than 160, the manager proceeds to add overtime pay. If not, the process moves directly to the next step.

Once the overtime pay is added, or if it was not needed, the manager calculates and checks both the gross pay and net pay for the employee. After verifying these amounts, the manager records all the details in a spreadsheet.

The accounting department then receives this working spreadsheet. They use it to prepare the payroll salary. After preparing the payroll, there is a waiting period of seven working days after the end of the month.

Following this waiting period, the accounting department sends the salary to the designated address for each employee. Once the salary is sent, the part-time employee receives their salary, marking the completion of the process.

The process begins when a tenant expresses the need for a damage repair. This request is initiated by the tenant and handled by HGF. Following this, HGF conducts preliminary checks to assess the situation.

Next, a decision is made to determine if the tenant is eligible for support from HGF. If the tenant is not eligible, HGF provides general advice to the tenant, and the process concludes. If the tenant is eligible, HGF gathers detailed information about the tenant, the flat, and the property owner (PO). Subsequently, HGF collects information regarding the specific repair needs.

Once all necessary information is gathered, HGF analyzes it to verify the legitimacy of the claim. If the claim is deemed illegitimate, HGF informs the tenant that the repair cannot be funded by the PO, and the process ends. If the claim is legitimate, HGF decides whether to demand a full or partial repair.

Following this decision, HGF begins negotiations with the PO. A further decision point arises to determine if an agreement with the PO is reached. If an agreement is reached, HGF is notified once the PO has completed the repair, and the process concludes. If no agreement is reached, and if the tenant wishes, the matter can be taken to court, after which the process ends.

The process begins when a student receives a project confirmation along with a link. The student then accesses the portal using this link. Upon accessing the portal, the student views a model that is not populated with QUT data. Next, the student views the guidelines on the landing page, which include prerequisites.

The student must agree to the guidelines and accept the IP deed and student declaration. After agreeing, the student creates an account using their QUT email. This action triggers the project management system to register the account. The system then looks up team invitations and requests either a team invite or the creation of a new team.

The student receives a request and encounters a decision point. If no team has been created yet, the student creates a team in the system. This prompts the project management system to register the team and assign the user to the team. The student then invites team members.

If a team already exists, the student accepts the invite, and the project management system registers the user to the team. Following this, the student begins the document process according to the guidelines.

The process then splits into two parallel tasks. The student completes iLearn certifications and fills out a vaccination form simultaneously. Once both tasks are completed, the student uploads the documents to the system.

The project management system receives the documents and checks for any pre-existing documents that may need updating. If updates are necessary, the student adds comments and confirms the upload. The project management system assigns comments to the documents and then assigns the documents to the student's user profile.

Finally, the process concludes with the project management system marking the end of the process.

The process begins when the scheduler initiates the scheduling of a course by clicking on "start scheduling" for the course. The scheduler then defines the course details. Following this, the scheduler assigns an instructor to the course. Once the instructor is assigned, the scheduler creates a new section for the course. After the section is created, the scheduler assigns a classroom for the course. Subsequently, the scheduler assigns a time slot for the course.

At this point, there is a decision to be made. If everything is in order, the scheduler sends out a message indicating that the course is created. This message leads to the course becoming active, allowing students to register. The process then ends successfully.

Alternatively, if there is an issue, an error message pops up. The scheduler then saves the information for later, and the process ends without the course being activated.

Separately, when a student is placed on a waiting list, the scheduler checks the number of students on the list. If there are more than 10 students, the scheduler creates a new section and assigns a classroom and time slot, similar to the initial process. If there are fewer than 10 students, the scheduler advises the student to wait until the next semester, and the process ends.

In another scenario, a student searches for a desired class and clicks on "register." If the class has available space, the student is enrolled, and the instructor is notified. The class space is then reduced accordingly. If the class is full, the student is placed on a waiting list, and the process follows the waiting list path described earlier.

The process begins with a general worker receiving fish from a conveyor belt. The worker then places the fish in a hopper scale to record its weight. This information is also sent to the Innova IT system.

Next, the general worker checks the fish for any external defects. If defects are found, which happens 5% of the time, the filleting operator removes the defective parts. If no defects are found, which occurs 95% of the time, the fish is passed to a quality inspector for further examination.

The quality inspector checks the fish against quality specifications. If the fish meets the specifications, which is the case 87% of the time, the inspector records the specifications and sends this information to the Innova IT system. The fish is then filleted into different parts by the filleting operator.

If the fish does not meet the quality specifications, which happens 13% of the time, the quality inspector discards the fish, ending the process for that batch.

After filleting, the filleting operator weighs the final parts. The quality inspector then assigns a quality assurance grade to the fish. Finally, the fish is sent to the packaging department, concluding the process.

The process begins when a customer initiates contact with Domino's Pizza. The customer calls to place an order, and a clerk at Domino's Pizza answers the call to take the order details. Once the order is received, the clerk proceeds to place the customer's order into the system.

After the order is placed, the clerk must determine the method of order fulfillment. There are two possible paths: delivery or takeout. If the order is for delivery, the clerk asks the customer if they want the order delivered. If the order is for takeout, the clerk asks the customer if they will pick up the order themselves.

Once the method of fulfillment is confirmed, the order is officially placed. Jane Doe, a staff member at Domino's Pizza, then prepares the pizza order. After preparation, Jane Doe bakes the pizza. Following the baking process, Jane Doe examines the quality of the pizza to ensure it meets Domino's standards.

When the pizza is ready, Jane Doe confirms its readiness. At this point, another decision is made regarding the order's next step. If the order is for delivery, it is carried out by a delivery vehicle. If the order is for takeout, it is prepared for customer pickup.

Finally, the process concludes when the order is either delivered to the customer or picked up by the customer, marking the end of the transaction.

The process begins with the department initiating the procedure. The first task for the department is to send a consent document to the lawyer. Once the lawyer receives the consent, they proceed to make an appointment. At this point, the lawyer checks if the partner is available to attend the meeting.

If the partner is not available, the lawyer makes a new appointment and sends a warning to the partner company. The warning is also communicated to an external brand lawyer. After sending the warning, the lawyer checks again if the partner agrees to attend. If the partner still does not agree, the process loops back to making another appointment. If the partner agrees, the lawyer establishes the contract.

Once the contract is established, the lawyer makes a copy of the original contract and sends it back to the department. The department then sends the contract to the CEO for signing. After the CEO signs the contract, they communicate back to the department to make an appointment.

The department then appoints a meeting and proceeds to announce the partnership. Finally, the process concludes with the department ending the procedure.

The process begins when a user encounters an issue. The user first checks the Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) to understand the nature of the issue. After reviewing the SOP, the user decides on the type of issue they are dealing with.

Next, the user reaches a decision point to determine if the issue requires a service request. If the answer is yes, the user fills out a service request form and submits it to their manager. The manager then receives the request and analyzes it. If the manager approves the request, it is implemented by the help desk, and the process concludes with the request being completed.

If the manager does not approve the request, the process ends with the request being declined.

If the issue does not require a service request, the help desk receives the request directly. The help desk then forwards the request to the appropriate group, and the process ends with the request being completed.

Alternatively, if the issue is directed to the web solutions team, they receive the request and work on rectifying the issues. Once the issues are resolved, the web solutions team notifies the user, and the process concludes with the request being completed.

The business process begins with GBI Global initiating the procedure by checking suppliers. Once the suppliers are checked, the process moves to the task of checking materials. After the materials are checked, the next step is to check the inventory.

Following the inventory check, GBI Global creates a purchase requisition. This leads to managing stock, which is followed by creating a request for quotation. Once the request for quotation is created, the process involves maintaining quotations from vendors.

After maintaining the quotations, GBI Global evaluates the quotations based on price. If the request for quotation is accepted, a purchase order is created referencing the request for quotation. This is followed by displaying the purchase order.

Next, GBI Global creates a goods receipt for the purchase order, which results in the generation of a material document. The process then involves managing stock again. After managing stock, an invoice receipt is created.

Subsequently, GBI Global verifies and displays the purchase documents. At this point, a decision is made: if the documents are verified successfully, a supplier invoice is created. If not, the process returns to creating a goods receipt for the purchase order.

Once the supplier invoice is created, payments are posted to the vendor. After posting payments, the documents are displayed, and the process concludes with the process being finished.

The process begins when an international student decides they want a U.S. driver's license. The first step involves the student bringing all necessary materials and filling out an application form. These two tasks are performed simultaneously.

Once the student has completed these tasks, the application form and materials are checked at Counter A by the MVC. If the application is approved, the student proceeds to fill in a new application form. If the application is denied, the process ends with the application failing.

After filling in the new application form, the student must make a payment. Following the payment, the MVC arranges an exam for the student. The student then takes the exam.

Once the exam is completed, the MVC checks the results. If the student does not pass, the process ends with the application failing. If the student passes, they proceed to pay and have their photograph taken.

After the payment and photograph, the MVC issues a new driver's license. Finally, the student receives their new driver's license, marking the end of the process.

The process begins with the Delivery Department of the Supplier initiating the task of sending the product. Once the product is sent, the Inventory Department at Yik Hong Enterprise receives it. Upon receiving the product, the Inventory Department requests a purchase order.

Next, the Purchasing Department at Yik Hong Enterprise searches for the purchase order. After locating the purchase order, the Inventory Department views both the purchase and delivery orders. They then check if the delivery order matches the purchase order. If there is no match, the process loops back to searching for the purchase order again. If there is a match, the Inventory Department proceeds to check the quality and quantity of the goods.

The Inventory Department then evaluates whether the quality and quantity match the expectations. If they do not match, the goods are returned to the Supplier. If they do match, the Inventory Department checks if the amount is greater than or equal to 10,000. If the amount is less than 10,000, the Inventory Department signs the delivery order document. If the amount is 10,000 or more, manager approval is required before signing the delivery order document.

After signing the delivery order document, the Inventory Department prints a barcode on the goods. The goods are then packaged and stored in the inventory. Following this, the inventory stock is updated. The Purchasing Department receives the updated stock level, marking the end of the process with the stock level being updated.

The process begins with the customer initiating contact with Longsoap. After this initial contact, the customer faces a decision point regarding planning for loved ones. If the customer decides to plan for loved ones, they proceed to a task where they address the loss of loved ones. If the customer chooses not to plan for loved ones, they move to a task where they plan a funeral for themselves.

Following either decision, the customer proceeds to choose a product. After selecting a product, the customer inserts the necessary information. Once the information is inserted, the customer chooses a payment method.

After choosing the payment method, the customer encounters another decision point about whether they are planning for themselves. If the answer is yes, the customer confirms they are still alive and then waits for a period. After waiting, the customer reaches a task labeled "RIP," which leads to contacting the supplier.

If the customer is not planning for themselves, they directly contact the supplier. The Longsoap staff then prepares for the next steps. Once preparation is complete, the funeral is started, and there is a waiting period. After the wait, the Longsoap staff handles the after-funeral ceremony, concluding the process.

The process begins at Harokopeio University. Initially, the university's administration requests topics from Jane Doe. This task is followed by another request for topics from Jane Doe, ensuring all necessary information is gathered.

Next, a parallel action occurs where professors send their topics to the administration for Jane Doe. This task is executed simultaneously by two different actors within the university. Once the topics are received, they are collected by the administration.

Following the collection of topics, the university publishes invitations for PhD thesis submissions. This step leads to two possible paths: one involves the publication of undergraduate thesis topics, and the other involves a waiting period marked by an intermediate timer event.

If the path of publishing undergraduate thesis topics is taken, the process continues with a student, referred to as "Foititis," reviewing the list of available graduate thesis topics. The student then engages in a discussion with a professor to select a suitable topic. After selecting a topic, the student uploads the chosen topic, which is communicated back to the university administration for verification.

Meanwhile, the university administration conducts a check of the submitted documents. If everything is in order, they proceed to contact the student via phone to discuss any necessary details. After this communication, the results are posted, marking the end of the process for the university.

The process for the student concludes once the topic is uploaded and verified, marking the end of their involvement.

Overall, this process involves multiple interactions between the university administration, professors, and students, ensuring a thorough and collaborative approach to managing thesis topics.

The process begins when a customer decides to rent a locker. The customer starts by opening a mobile app. Once the app is open, the customer searches for available locker locations and sizes. The system then displays the available options based on the customer's search criteria.

Next, the customer checks if a suitable locker is available. If no suitable locker is found, the customer closes the app, ending the process. If a suitable locker is available, the customer selects a locker. The system then starts a 15-minute reservation for the locker and generates a QR barcode, which is displayed to the customer. The system confirms to the customer that the locker is booked.

The customer then scans the reservation QR barcode. The system checks if more than 15 minutes have passed since the reservation. If it has, the system sends a notice that the locker reservation has expired, and the process returns to the search step. If it has not been more than 15 minutes, the customer is presented with three options: enter login information, create a new user account, or continue without a user account.

If the customer chooses to enter login information, they proceed to enter the booking duration. If they choose to create a new user account, they do so before entering the booking duration. If they choose to continue without a user account, they directly enter the booking duration. The system then calculates the booking price and displays the booking price and duration to the customer.

The customer accepts the booking price and duration. The system prompts the customer to enter their cellphone number for the locker pin. The customer enters their cellphone number, and the system starts the payment process. The customer inserts their credit card PIN codes, and the system processes the transaction.

After the transaction is processed, the system prints the PIN code and opens the reserved locker. The customer places their items in the locker and closes the door, completing the process.

The process begins with the Job Portal System logging into the Job Seeker's Main Page. Once logged in, the system displays the main page for the job seeker. From here, the Employee User is prompted to select a choice. The user can either choose to view the message inbox or configure settings.

If the Employee User decides to view the message inbox, they click the "Message Inbox" button. This action prompts the Job Portal System to display all messages in the inbox. The Employee User then checks the messages. At this point, they must decide whether to view the message details. If they choose to view the details, they select a message, and the system displays the message detail. After viewing, the Employee User can click the "Back" button to return to the inbox display.

If the Employee User decides not to view the message details, they can click the "Exit" button, which takes them back to the Job Seeker's Main Page. This concludes the process for viewing messages.

Alternatively, if the Employee User chooses to configure settings, they proceed to configure the setting for receiving message inbox notifications. Once configured, the Job Portal System saves the setting. The system then checks the configuration to determine if notifications are enabled. If enabled, the system sends a message inbox notification. Regardless of the decision, the process ends after this step.

Throughout the process, the Job Portal System manages data storage for the message inbox, main page, and applicant information, ensuring that all necessary data is available for each task.

The process begins with the user logging in. Once logged in, the user selects "services" from the available options. After choosing "services," the user then picks a specific field of services they are interested in.

At this point, the user encounters a decision point where they must choose between three options: HR services, real estate services, or other services. 

1. If the user selects HR services, they proceed to pick a specific HR service. After selecting the HR service, the user faces another decision point. Here, they can either choose to leave, which leads to executing a leave service, or select another option, which redirects them to define the service in short.

2. If the user chooses real estate services, they pick a specific real estate service. This choice leads to executing the real estate service.

3. If the user opts for other services, they define the service briefly. Following this, the user describes the problem or service in detail. Next, the user describes what they want, which generates a message sent to the service provider.

Once the service provider receives the request, they execute the service and notify the user. The notification is sent back to the user, completing the process.

The process concludes with the user receiving a notification, marking the end of the process. Each path through the process ends with a distinct conclusion, depending on the choices made by the user.

The process begins when the accounting team sends an email, which is received by the accounting data validation team. This initial task is handled by a default actor.

Next, the data validation team pulls data from the accounting system. This task is also managed by a default actor. After retrieving the data from the accounting system, the team proceeds to pull data from the PnA system.

Once data from both systems is gathered, the team validates the data between the accounting system and the PnA system. This ensures consistency and accuracy between the two data sources.

Following the validation, the process reaches a point where two tasks occur simultaneously. The first task involves validating and cleaning the Tie Out Sheet. The second task is the audit submission. Both tasks are carried out by default actors.

After the Tie Out Sheet is validated and cleaned, the data is sent for CA validation. This marks the end of the process.

Meanwhile, after the audit submission, the data is validated between the accounting system and the GPA-NGA system. This step ensures that the data aligns correctly between these systems. Once this validation is complete, the data is also sent for CA validation, concluding the process.

The process begins with a PhD student starting the seminar presentation. The first step involves the student registering online or sending an email to A.C. Once this is completed, the student moves on to designate two discussants for the seminar.

After designating the discussants, the student prepares to present their paper and a PowerPoint presentation. Following this preparation, the student reserves a room for the presentation.

Once the room is reserved, the process reaches a point where two tasks occur simultaneously. The student must bring a laptop with the presentation to the seminar and also send the paper to all participants. These tasks are carried out in parallel.

If the paper is sent to participants more than two weeks before the presentation, there is a waiting period until two weeks before the presentation. At that point, the student sends the papers immediately to ensure all participants have the necessary materials.

After these tasks are completed, the student proceeds to present the seminar. Following the presentation, the student draws up a written report. This report is then used to update a booklet related to the seminar.

The process concludes with the end of the seminar presentation. Throughout the process, the PhD student is responsible for each task, ensuring that all steps are completed in a timely and organized manner.

The process begins with the stove being assembled by the production line. Once the stove is assembled, the production line fills in the stove information, which includes details such as the guarantee number, model, options, and client references. This information is documented in a production quality sheet.

Next, the production line checks and tests the stove's components to ensure they are functioning correctly. Following this, the engine of the stove is switched on to verify that it works well. If the engine works well, the process continues with two tasks happening simultaneously: the stove is cleaned properly, and any dirt residue is removed. Both tasks are performed by the production line.

After cleaning, the production line sticks an A++ label and marks the CE label on the stove's door. The CE label indicates European Conformity. The production line then fills in the rest of the quality sheet.

If the engine does not work well, the production line uses a QR code to find any missing or misplaced pieces. This task is supported by an IT system. Once the issue is identified, the production line fixes it and then rechecks the engine to ensure it works well.

After the labeling and quality sheet tasks are completed, the production line adds an instruction sheet, plan, and items list to the stove. The stove is then packaged, and the process concludes with the product being operational and ready to leave the production line.

The process begins with the Purchasing Department at Chan Sang Enterprise initiating the procedure. The first step involves the department logging into the system. Once logged in, the system displays the main menu, managed by SAP B1.

The Purchasing Department then selects an option from the menu. This leads to a decision point where the department must choose between several actions: checking stock, requesting a purchase requisition, requesting a purchase order, or receiving goods.

If the department chooses to check stock, SAP B1 retrieves the stock details, and the department reads these details. This path concludes the process.

If the department opts to request a purchase requisition, they enter the necessary information, which SAP B1 verifies. If the information is verified, SAP B1 generates the purchase requisition and saves it. The system then displays a vendor list, and the department selects a vendor. Following this, the department requests a quotation, which SAP B1 sends to the vendor. Upon receiving the quotation, SAP B1 compares it, and this path concludes the process.

Choosing to request a purchase order leads to another decision point where the department must decide if there is a reference. If there is no reference, the department enters the purchase order information, which SAP B1 verifies. If verified, the purchase order is placed, sent, and this path concludes the process. If there is a reference, the purchase order is placed directly, sent, and this path also concludes the process.

If the department decides to receive goods, they check the quantity and quality of the goods. SAP B1 then saves a goods receipt note and a quality report, concluding this path of the process.

Throughout the process, SAP B1 plays a crucial role in managing and verifying information, ensuring that each step is completed accurately and efficiently. The process ends with various outcomes depending on the path taken by the Purchasing Department.

The process begins when a request is received by the IT Helpdesk, handled by Level 1 Staff. This request can come through either a call or an email. Once the request is received, Level 1 Staff registers the new request in the system.

After registration, the process reaches a decision point where Level 1 Staff determines whether the issue is a known problem or an unknown one. If it is a known issue, which happens 80% of the time, Level 1 Staff checks the problem and then communicates the resolution to the client. Once the client is informed, the case is considered resolved and the process ends.

If the issue is unknown, which occurs 20% of the time, the request is escalated to Level 2 Staff. Level 2 Staff first evaluates and assigns a priority level to the request. Then, they assign the request to themselves for further investigation. They conduct research to find a resolution and then write down the resolution. After documenting the resolution, Level 2 Staff sends it to the client. The resolution is then forwarded to the client, who tests the solution.

Once the client tests the solution, they send an email back to the IT Helpdesk. At this point, another decision is made. If the problem is resolved, which is the case 90% of the time, Level 1 Staff confirms that the problem is resolved, and the case is marked as complete. If the problem remains unresolved, which happens 10% of the time, the request is forwarded to Level 2 Staff again, and the case is marked as incomplete.

Throughout this process, Level 1 Staff handles known issues and initial client communication, while Level 2 Staff deals with unknown issues and more complex problem-solving. The process ensures that all requests are addressed efficiently, with clear communication between the IT Helpdesk and the client.

The process begins with a staff member at A123 Sdn Bhd initiating the task of filling in a travel expense report. Once the report is completed, the staff member proceeds to attach all relevant travel documents to the report. This results in the creation of a claim document.

Next, the supervisor at A123 Sdn Bhd takes over to verify the submitted claim. After verification, the supervisor must decide whether to approve or reject the claim. If the claim is approved, the supervisor sends it forward. If the claim is rejected, the supervisor informs the staff member about the rejection, and the process ends there.

If the claim amount is greater than or equal to 10,000, the process requires further approval from a senior manager. The senior manager then decides to either approve or reject the claim. If approved, the senior manager proceeds to approve the claim. If rejected, the senior manager rejects the claim. Regardless of the decision, the process continues to a parallel gateway.

At the parallel gateway, two actions occur simultaneously. The account department is informed about the collection, and they prepare for payment. Once the payment is prepared, the account department informs the relevant parties about the collection, and the claim is reimbursed, marking the end of the process.

The business process begins at Sy's Fish store, where an employee answers the phone. After answering the phone, the employee prepares a refund authorization. Once the refund authorization is prepared, the process reaches a point where two actions occur simultaneously.

First, if the customer has not paid, the store employee informs the customer to remove the charge from their bill. Following this, the employee sends a return authorization to Sy.

Second, if the customer has paid, the store employee informs the customer that they will receive a check. The employee then sends the refund authorization to Natalie, the accounts payable clerk.

Natalie, the accounts payable clerk, receives the refund authorization. She then sends a check to the customer. After sending the check, Natalie sends the payment information to Sy.

Finally, Sy receives the payment information, marking the end of the process.

The business process begins when DAC Jane Doe receives a purchase order. Upon receiving the order, Jane creates a sales order in the SAP system. Next, Jane checks if the goods are available in stock.
